title: Anger on the road
hookLine: traffic, queues, delays: where anger strikes
tomorrow: the road was hard. why is home even harder?

cards: Tuesday afternoon. Simran hasn't had her license long, Bebe is in the passenger seat with her ankle in a boot, and they're late for physical therapy. A truck swings into her lane without a signal.

Her foot slams the brake, her hands go white on the wheel, her heart pounds in her ears, and her mouth is already open with a word Bebe has never heard her say. Behind them, someone leans on a horn, as if it's her fault.
Bebe doesn't flinch. She puts one hand flat on the dashboard and says one word: saah. Breath.

teach.b: The Sikh word for that heat is krodh: anger. On ang 600, Guru Amar Das names five thieves that live inside the body, lust, anger, greed, attachment and pride, and says they steal the nectar while we don't notice.
On ang 1358, Guru Arjan speaks to anger directly, in paraphrase: O anger, root of strife, you have no mercy; you make people dance like monkeys. Here's what's worth repeating.
The Guru doesn't describe anger as an opinion. He describes something that grabs the body and makes it dance.
That matches the car exactly: the foot, the hands, the heartbeat, the open mouth, all before a single sentence forms. So the first answer to this thief is in the body too.
The breath is the one part of that rush we can steer. One slow breath doesn't make the truck driver right. It makes Simran the driver of her own car again.
The same is true in a slow line at the pharmacy, or stuck on hold: the body goes first, so the breath goes first.
Breathe first; think second. Simran breathes out, long and slow.
The truck is gone. Bebe lifts her hand off the dashboard and says, almost to herself, Waheguru. They get to therapy a few minutes late, and nobody minds.
On the way home, Simran drives a little slower, and Bebe turns the radio on.

how: Sikhs speak of anger (krodh) as one of the five thieves; many repeat Waheguru or a line of Gurbani under their breath to steady themselves in a hard moment.

games.q: what does “anger on the road” mean?
o: anger that flares in traffic, lines and delays
a sign the other driver deserves to be stopped
a kind of anger that only comes from tiredness

games.q: the thief on the road — tap the pairs.
p: anger, one of the five thieves
five thieves living in the body

s: road rage is mostly in the head, so the answer is better thinking
the Guru describes anger grabbing the body and making it dance; the first answer is the breath.
Guru Amar Das names anger among five thieves that live inside the body
ang 600: lust, anger, greed, attachment and pride, stealing the nectar.
the breath works by proving the other driver was wrong
one slow breath doesn't make the truck driver right; it makes you the driver of your own car again.

games.q: you're in a long line at the pharmacy and the person ahead is arguing about a coupon. your jaw is tight and a sharp line is ready. what does today's lesson say comes first?
o: a long, slow breath out, before any words.
a calm, clear explanation of why they're wrong.
leaving the line before you say something.
games.why: anger grabs the body first, on ang 1358 it makes people dance, so the first move is in the body too: breathe first.

practice: Rest your hands on your knees as if on a wheel, and squeeze them tight for a moment; feel the heat in your arms and jaw. Then let go and breathe out slowly, longer than you breathed in.
Keep that long out-breath going, hands open, and feel the body settle.

wordCard.voice: Anger on the road. Krodh, one of the five thieves, grabbing the body first, and the breath that answers it.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: krodh, anger, one of the five thieves named on ang 600.

carryVoice: Breathe first: the thief grabs the body, so let the body answer first. Drive gently out there.

sources.ref: Ang 600 (Sorath, Mahala 3: is dehee andar panch chor vaseh kaam krodh lobh moh ahankaaraa; amrit lootteh), paraphrased
Ang 1358 (Salok Sahaskriti, Mahala 5: he kal mool krodhang, the salok addressed to anger), paraphrased
